title: Stop Sweeping It Under the Rug! – Revealing the Hidden Phases and Elements of 2D Material Interfaces with Atom Probe Tomography
content: Atom probe tomography (APT) has emerged as a transformative tool for achieving atomic-scale, three-dimensional compositional analysis. While its application has been widely demonstrated for needle-shaped specimens, extending APT to two-dimensional (2D) materials and thin films presents unique challenges due to their distinctive mechanical, electrical, and bonding properties. The high electric fields required for APT can induce significant Maxwell stresses, leading to specimen fracture, especially in 2D systems stabilized by weak van der Waals forces. Due to these challenges, until recently 2D materials needed to be embedded within a matrix to stabilize the structure [1]. The development of in situ sputtering of metals (i.e. chromium) has been instrumental in facilitating APT of 2D systems, including MXene films [2]. Beyond structural and compositional analysis, APT’s exceptional ability to detect light elements with high spatial resolution further solidifies its utility in understanding 2D systems, where light elements often play a pivotal role in material properties. This work highlights the development and application of APT for 2D thin films and freestanding 2D oxides, with a particular emphasis on its role in detecting critical nanoscale compositional features, including light elements, that are challenging to capture with other techniques. Furthermore, we integrate APT with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to provide complementary structural and chemical analysis, leveraging the strengths of both techniques to achieve a comprehensive understanding of these systems.
